lines.text:
Surviving the Heat — Life in the Desert

The desert looks empty, but it is full of life. Animals, plants, and even people have found ways to survive in one of the harshest environments on Earth — where the hot sun beats down during the day, and cool nights bring a sharp drop in temperature.

The landscape is dramatic. Tall sand dunes curve across the horizon. A canyon cuts deep into the rock. A mesa — a flat-topped hill — stands alone against the sky. A butte is smaller than a mesa but just as striking. In the distance, a plateau stretches for kilometres. A dry riverbed shows where water once flowed. Somewhere out there, an oasis — a small area with water and palm trees — gives life to travellers and animals. A rocky outcrop provides shade. A crater marks where a meteorite hit the ground thousands of years ago. A basin collects rainwater after rare storms.

Desert animals have adapted to survive with very little water. A camel can drink over 100 litres at once and survive for days without more. A fennec fox — the world's smallest fox — has enormous ears that release body heat. A meerkat stands on its back legs to watch for hawks and vultures circling above. A rattlesnake rests under a rock during the day and hunts at night. A scorpion hides in the sand. A lizard runs across the hot surface at incredible speed. A tortoise moves slowly but stores water inside its body. A roadrunner — a bird that prefers running to flying — chases lizards along the ground. An armadillo rolls into a ball when threatened. A coyote howls at the moon.

Desert plants are just as clever. A cactus stores water in its thick stem. A barrel cactus is round and covered in sharp spines. A prickly pear has flat pads and produces edible fruit. A Joshua tree — found only in the American Southwest — has unusual twisted branches. An aloe and an agave store water in their thick leaves. Sage brush and tumbleweed survive in the driest conditions. A date palm grows near an oasis and produces sweet fruit.

Travel in the desert requires preparation. A water canteen is essential — dehydration is the biggest danger. A sun hat and sunscreen protect against sunburn. Sunglasses reduce the glare. A compass and a map help with navigation — there are few landmarks in open desert. Shade is rare, so a tent provides shelter during the hottest hours. A first aid kit treats cuts and bites. A water filter can make found water safe to drink.

Desert weather is extreme. A sandstorm can reduce visibility to zero in minutes. A heat wave pushes temperatures above 50°C. A mirage — a visual trick caused by hot air — makes distant sand look like water. Drought — long periods without rain — is normal. The dry air means the sky is often perfectly clear, which is why some of the world's best observatories are built in deserts.

The desert teaches patience, preparation, and respect for nature. Everything that lives here has learned to make the most of very little.

lines.text: Short adjectives (one syllable) use '-er' for comparatives: 'hot → hotter', 'big → bigger', 'cold → colder.' Longer adjectives use 'more': 'more dangerous', 'more beautiful.' Never 'more hot' or 'more cold' — these are one-syllable words.

lines.text: After 'can', 'could', 'must', 'should', 'will', 'may', and 'might', use the bare infinitive — no 'to.' 'It can survive.' 'They must drink.' 'We should prepare.' This is one of the most important grammar rules at B1.

lines.text: 'Few' + countable plural: 'few animals', 'few plants.' 'Little' + uncountable: 'little water', 'little shade.' 'A few' = some (positive): 'There are a few oases.' 'A little' = some (positive): 'There is a little water.' 'Few/little' (no article) = almost none.

lines.text: 'Drink – drank – drunk.' 'Drank' is the past simple: 'It drank the water yesterday.' 'Drunk' is the past participle: 'It has drunk all the water.' This pattern is like 'sing – sang – sung' and 'swim – swam – swum.' Many irregular verbs follow this a–a–u vowel pattern.

lines.text: 'Be used to + noun/-ing' = be accustomed to: 'I'm not used to the heat.' 'She's used to walking in the sun.' Don't confuse with 'used to + infinitive' (past habit): 'I used to live in the desert.' The structure changes: 'be used to' (present habit) vs. 'used to' (past habit).

lines.text: 'Desert' /ˈdezət/ = dry land (stress on first syllable). 'Dessert' /dɪˈzɜːt/ = sweet course (stress on second syllable). Also: 'to desert' /dɪˈzɜːt/ (verb) = to abandon. 'Just deserts' = what someone deserves.

lines.text: The Sahara (Africa) is the largest hot desert. The Arabian Desert covers much of the Middle East. The Gobi (Asia) is a cold desert. Antarctica is technically the largest desert — it receives very little precipitation.

lines.text: The Bedouin are nomadic Arab peoples of the desert. They traditionally live in tents made of goat hair. Hospitality is a core value — offering coffee and dates to guests is customary. Many Bedouin communities now live in settled towns.

lines.text: 'Aquifer' = underground layer of water-bearing rock. 'Well' = a hole dug to reach underground water. 'Spring' = where water naturally flows to the surface. 'Reservoir' = artificial lake for water storage. These are useful B2 vocabulary items.
